title: Sam Sails Through the Parade
learning_objectives: Explain why Sam kept the chairs and changed his costume idea
Connect the upright paper wings with the imagined ship

rights.text_author: GitHub Copilot for Read Oasis (original, AI-authored)

parent_prompts: Before reading: How could paper help Sam pretend to sail through a parade?
After page 3: Why does Sam want to keep the chairs even though his wings bump them?
After reading: How did the same folded paper become part of a different parade?

pages.text: Sam folded two wide wings for his paper costume. In the pretend parade, he would fly above the houses.
pages.image_alt: Sam presses a fold into one of two pale paper wings at a low table while Mo watches.

vocabulary.definition: Clothes or things worn to pretend.
vocabulary.example: My paper costume makes me a ship.

pages.text: Sam turned with his paper wings spread wide. Both wings bumped the chairs beside the narrow parade path.
pages.image_alt: Sam turns between two chairs with wide folded paper wings touching the chair backs and paper people on the seats.

vocabulary.definition: Having little space from side to side.
vocabulary.example: Wide wings cannot fit along the narrow path.

pages.text: Sam wanted to keep the chairs beside the path. They were houses for his paper people to watch the parade.
pages.image_alt: Sam crouches beside a chair and touches a little paper person while his wide paper wings lie on the floor near Mo.

pages.audio_script: Sam wanted to keep the chairs beside the path. They were houses for his paper people to watch the parade.

pages.text: Sam lifted both wings above his shoulders. They fitted between the chairs, but no longer looked like wings.

pages.text: Mo looked up at the tall paper folds. Their pointed shadows made Sam imagine sails catching the wind.

vocabulary.example: Sam pretends his paper wings are sails.

pages.text: Sam could be a ship! Holding the same folded paper upright as sails, he called the path a river.

quiz.prompt: Why did Sam keep the chairs after his wings bumped them?

options.text: They belonged in his pretend town
They helped his paper wings stay wide
They kept Mo away from the parade

quiz.explanation: Page 2 says the wings bumped the chairs. Page 3 explains why Sam kept them: they were houses for the paper people watching his parade.

quiz.prompt: Why did Sam choose a ship after raising his paper wings?

options.text: Mo asked him to build a ship
He wanted to copy the paper people
The upright paper fitted and suggested sails

quiz.explanation: Page 4 says the raised paper fitted but no longer looked like wings. Its shadows suggest sails on page 5, so Sam imagines being a ship on page 6.

quiz.prompt: Why is Sam pleased with his new plan?

options.text: Mo can now wear his paper wings
His town stays in the pretend parade
He no longer needs his paper costume

quiz.explanation: Page 3 establishes that Sam wants to keep the chair houses for his paper people. Page 7 keeps them untouched, and page 8 shows he is glad they can still enjoy the parade: keeping his town matters more than the original flying costume.

quiz.prompt: Tell how Sam changed his flying costume into a ship while keeping the paper people in their houses.
quiz.rubric: not yet: names wings or sails without explaining the change; with support: tells that wide wings bumped chairs and upright paper fitted; independent: connects keeping the chair houses, raising the wings, noticing sail shadows, and sailing along the pretend river.
quiz.explanation: The explanation should preserve the reason for keeping the chairs and show how the same paper supports the new ship idea.

activities.prompt: Put the wing problem and ship parade in order.

items.text: Paper shadows give Sam a sail idea.
Wide paper wings bump the chairs.
Sam sails around the river bend.
Sam raises the wings above his shoulders.

prompts: Why would moving the chairs have changed the pretend parade Sam wanted?
Which matters more to Sam at the end: keeping his flying costume or keeping a parade for the paper people?

off_screen_prompt: Fold a sheet of paper and imagine two different costumes it could become; tell a grown-up how your second idea changes the pretend place, as Sam changed a path into a river.
